title: Live control-room timing consumer edge
description: Objective: give the existing timing evaluator a REAL production consumer that feeds it observed timestamps, replacing the current state where only tests ever call it. Deliverable: the live control-room path records its own client-received and surface-rendered observations against an injected clock, carries the daemon's command identity through the live feed, and at least one actual live surface calls evaluateTiming/describeTimingReceipt with those observed values. SPIDR slice 2 of 3 from parent task-1eeb2dccce204671b442704cd60b38ad. HARD DEPENDENCY on sibling task-1430dfae1a0e4e8c88fafc7bf011ba9f, which puts command identity and daemon readings on the wire; re-measure that those fields exist on disk before planning against them and report blocked if absent. MEASURED AT HEAD 6ffb4fe (re-measure, this WILL be stale): apps/control-room/src/performance/timing.ts:162 evaluateTiming is pure and takes CALLER-SUPPLIED {start,end} pairs; grep shows its only call sites are command-latency.test.tsx and timing.test.ts - ZERO production callers. Production command-latency.tsx:5 imports only describeTimingReceipt and measureElapsed and receives the receipt as a PROP, so production renders a receipt it never computes. live-event-feed.ts:13 LiveEventRow is {aggregateId, committedAt, eventId, eventType, position} and its header states rows copy the wire fields and add nothing. measureElapsed already exists and already returns TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE with no clock - reuse it, do not write a second elapsed helper. KNOWN HAZARD: packages/control-room-client/src/generated/generated-client.ts is marked GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT BY HAND, source of truth @moe/contracts, regenerate with pnpm --filter @moe/control-room-client generate; if the client must carry new fields, that is a contracts+codegen task, so report blocked rather than hand-editing generated output. NOT in scope: daemon-side emission, decision-effort/attention/focus records, benchmark statistics or thresholds. Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test && pnpm --filter @moe/control-room-client test && pnpm typecheck.
definitionOfDone: At least one actual live control-room surface calls evaluateTiming and describeTimingReceipt with timestamps OBSERVED on the live path, not fixture values and not props supplied by a test; the call site is production code reachable from the live app.

Client-received and surface-rendered observations are recorded separately against an injected clock, and the live event rows carry the daemon's command identity so a receipt can be attributed to one command.
System latency and response time remain separate phases; no code path sums, averages or collapses the four named phases into one number.

A missing clock, a missing observation or a cross-clock pair yields the existing exact UNKNOWN code (TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE, TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE, TIMING_NEGATIVE_INTERVAL) with its observer - never zero, never an absolute value, never an interpolated duration.

Tests prove the REAL edge: a live-path test drives the production call site and asserts the rendered receipt, and a mutation that bypasses the production render timestamp turns a named live test red. Refusal tests pin exact code and observer; generated phase cases assert a nonzero exact cardinality covering every timing split.
Fresh pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test && pnpm --filter @moe/control-room-client test && pnpm typecheck exits 0.
taskRails: Do not hand-edit packages/control-room-client/src/generated/generated-client.ts; it is generated from @moe/contracts. If new client fields are needed, report blocked and name a contracts/codegen task.
Do not collapse server, stream/client receipt, render and human time; response time is not system latency.
Do not compare cross-machine timestamps without an explicit shared observer or clock-offset uncertainty; unresolved skew stays UNKNOWN.
Reuse the landed measureElapsed/fromInterval discipline in timing.ts rather than writing a second elapsed or skew helper.
Instrumentation is observational and grants no authority or evidence strength.
Target <=250 physical lines per production source and split before 400; the cap is per file.

implementationPlan.description: TDD. Extend the timing vocabulary so a cross-layer UNKNOWN stays attributable. Today TimingUnknown is {known:false, observedBy, reasonCode} with TimingUnknownCode a 4-member union (TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE, TIMING_NEGATIVE_INTERVAL, TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE) - there is nowhere to record that the DAEMON SEAM itself reported UNKNOWN, so a seam refusal would be indistinguishable from the control room failing to parse. Add one code (e.g. TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN) to both the union and TIMING_UNKNOWN_CODES, and add an OPTIONAL upstream carrier to TimingUnknown holding the seam's own exact code and layer verbatim - no translation table, matching how the event-stream seam already forwards store codes. I MEASURED that nothing pins the length of TIMING_UNKNOWN_CODES; only TIMING_PHASE_NAMES is pinned, as an exact 4-element array at timing.test.ts:124, and this step adds NO phase, so that assertion must stay green. Leave evaluateTiming, measureElapsed and fromInterval's ordering (absent, then unparseable, then skew) untouched.
implementationPlan.note:
Timing vocabulary extended. TDD: tests appended to timing.test.ts first, then timing.ts.

Added TWO codes, not one. Step 1 said "add one code (e.g. TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN)"; DoD-5 forces a second. DoD-5 enumerates "a cross-clock pair as its explicit UNKNOWN" and "no clock as TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE" as SEPARATE assertion arms, so they must be separately pinnable, so they cannot share a code. Reusing TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE for cross-clock would also be false (a clock was available — two were) and reusing TIMING_NEGATIVE_INTERVAL misattributes. So: TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH + TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN. TIMING_UNKNOWN_CODES is now 6, pinned by a hand-written literal.

Also added, all required by later steps:
- TimingUpstreamRefusal {code, layer}; optional `upstream` carrier on TimingUnknown, forwarded verbatim with no translation table (matches how the seam forwards store codes).
- TimingLine gains upstreamCode/upstreamLayer so the refusing layer survives all the way to the DOM. Without it a rendered line would say "another layer refused" and never say which.
- timingUnknown() exported (was the private `unknown()`): the bridge must build refusals with the same freeze shape and the same observer attribution rather than a second copy.
- OBSERVER renamed to exported TIMING_PHASE_OBSERVERS so the bridge attributes refusals from the SAME map the evaluator uses, not a drifting duplicate.

evaluateTiming, measureElapsed and fromInterval's ordering (absent, unparseable, skew) untouched. timing.test.ts:124 TIMING_PHASE_NAMES exact-4 assertion still green; no phase added.

Verify: npx vitest run src/performance/timing.test.ts -> 1 file, 26 tests passed, exit 0. timing.ts 231 lines (target 250).

implementationPlan.description: TDD. Create the wire-to-timing bridge in a new focused module. It converts the daemon's WireObservation {clock, observer, reading: WireKnownValue|WireUnknownValue} into something evaluateTiming can consume, and it is the ONLY place that conversion happens. Three rules, each a test: (1) a WireUnknownValue never becomes a number - it yields TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN carrying the seam's exact code and layer, never TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, because 'the daemon said it does not know' and 'we never received it' are different facts; (2) a WireKnownValue.value is a STRING and TimingInterval takes NUMBERS, so parse explicitly and refuse an unparseable reading with TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE rather than letting NaN flow onward; (3) THE LOAD-BEARING RULE - before subtracting two readings, compare their declared `clock` identities and refuse a cross-clock pair outright with an explicit UNKNOWN. Do NOT rely on fromInterval's `end < start` skew guard for this: that catches only the half of cross-clock skew that happens to go negative, while skew in the other direction produces a plausible, confidently WRONG duration. The wire now carries an explicit `clock` field precisely so this check is possible; use it.
implementationPlan.note:
Bridge landed at apps/control-room/src/performance/wire-timing.ts. TDD: wire-timing.test.ts written first.

All three rules implemented and each pinned by a test:
1. readWireObservation on a refused wire reading yields TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN carrying the seam's exact {code, layer} verbatim. A test asserts it is NOT the same code as an absent observation, so the two facts cannot silently merge.
2. Known readings are strings; parsed with Date.parse and refused with TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE when non-finite. No NaN flows onward. Swept over "", "not-a-timestamp", "2026-13-45T99:99:99Z".
3. pairing() compares declared clock identities BEFORE the pair is handed to evaluateTiming, which is the only place a subtraction happens. The load-bearing test uses FORWARD skew (seam 5s AFTER ledger, so end > start): the negative-interval guard cannot fire there, and the pair still refuses TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH. Backward direction asserted too.

NO cross-package import. apps/control-room declares no dependency on apps/daemon and readEventPage is an untyped passthrough, so the wire arrives as `unknown`. shapeWireObservation parses it structurally (same discipline as live-event-feed.ts rowOf): every field required, a malformed observation returns null rather than defaulting a clock or observer into something that looks attributable. This sidesteps the dependency-edge rail entirely - there is no edge to verify because none is used.

Attribution detail worth flagging: pairing() re-stamps each refusal with the PHASE's observer from TIMING_PHASE_OBSERVERS, not the reading's. A seam refusal that makes `stream` unmeasurable keeps stream=CONTROL_ROOM (the control room is who was watching for that interval) while the upstream carrier names SEAM. Without this the stream phase would have inherited DAEMON from the seam reading and misattributed the observer. Test pins both halves.

Physical consequence measured, not assumed: `server` (STORE_COMMIT_CLOCK vs DAEMON_WALL_CLOCK) and `stream` (DAEMON_WALL_CLOCK vs the browser clock) are BOTH necessarily cross-clock in production, so both refuse TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH. `render` (received -> rendered, both on the one injected clock) is the genuinely measurable phase. That matches the daemon's own event-stream-observation.ts header, which states the two daemon readings' difference "is not a duration".

FORCED EDIT: timing.test.ts PRODUCTION_MODULES is a CLOSED list asserted equal to readdirSync of src/performance. Adding a module there forces its one-line entry or the directory scan fails. Entry added with anchor "export function buildLiveTimingReceipt(". The new module also inherits that scan's no-real-clock ban for free, which is the right home for it.

implementationPlan.description: TDD. Carry command identity and the client-received observation through the live feed. LiveEventRow is today exactly {aggregateId, committedAt, eventId, eventType, position} and the module header states rows 'copy the wire fields and add nothing'. Extend it with the wire's identity (WireEventIdentity carries commandId plus principal/run/session as WireValue unions) and the two daemon observations, copied VERBATIM - the feed shapes, it never infers, and that header rule still holds: no truth class is invented and an absent field stays absent rather than becoming a default. Then record the CLIENT-RECEIVED observation at the moment the frame arrives, using an injected clock, and stamp it on the frame. Reuse the existing LiveFeedOptions.schedule injection precedent for testability - take the clock as an option rather than reading a host time API, so a feed with no clock records TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE instead of quietly reporting that no time passed. Preserve every existing connection/outcome behavior: DISCONNECTED with the transport code, CONNECTED carrying a daemon refusal verbatim, LIVE_FRAME_UNREADABLE for a malformed body.

implementationPlan.description: TDD. Land the REAL production consumer edge - DoD-1, and the whole point of this task. recovery-actions.tsx:241 renders `<CommandLatency clock={clock} feedback={entry} .../>` with NO receipt prop, and command-latency.tsx:146 reads `{receipt === undefined ? null : <PhaseLines .../>}`, so production today renders a receipt it never computes and the phase lines never appear at all. Compute a receipt in recovery-actions.tsx from OBSERVED values - the daemon observations carried on the live row, the client-received observation from step 3, and a render observation taken from the existing Clock (prop or ClockContext) - pass them through the step-2 bridge into evaluateTiming, and hand the result to CommandLatency as `receipt`. Match the receipt to the feedback entry by commandId, which entry already carries. The four phases stay separate: nothing may sum, average or collapse them, because a single total makes the four indistinguishable. If no clock is available the surface must still render, with the receipt showing TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE - a missing clock is a measurable fact, never a zero.

CHOSEN INSTEAD: the live timeline, which IS the live app. New module apps/control-room/src/live/live-command-timing.tsx renders CommandLatency with a receipt built from OBSERVED values; live-app.tsx LiveTimeline renders <LiveCommandTiming frame={frame} /> and LiveControlRoom passes the composition root's clock into createLiveEventFeed. Chain now proven end to end: main.tsx -> LiveControlRoom -> LiveTimeline -> LiveCommandTiming -> buildLiveTimingReceipt -> evaluateTiming, and CommandLatency -> describeTimingReceipt. Put in a new module rather than inline so live-app.tsx stays at 230 lines (target 250).

Every input is observed, none is a prop a caller chose: the two daemon readings ride the row the daemon sent; the client-received reading was taken by the feed at arrival; the render reading is read from the injected clock during render (never stored in state - StrictMode-safe, same discipline command-latency.tsx documents).

Attribution: a receipt is built from the row carrying that commandId and rendered under testIdPrefix cr.live.timing.<commandId>, so one receipt maps to exactly one command. A row with no identity gets NO receipt rather than one attached to a guess - pinned by a test.

WHAT THE PRODUCTION RECEIPT HONESTLY REPORTS, measured not assumed: render measures (both readings on the one injected clock, asserted = 30ms). server refuses TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH (store commit clock vs daemon wall clock) and stream refuses TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH (daemon wall clock vs browser monotonic clock). That is not missing wiring - it is the daemon's own event-stream-observation.ts header enforced ("their difference is not a duration"), and main.tsx's own comment that the monotonic origin is never compared to a daemon timestamp. human stays TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT until an operator acts. No sum, no average, no total anywhere.

Also: exported useClock() from command-latency.tsx (ClockContext was private, so a live surface had no way to take its own reading), and PhaseLines now renders data-upstream-code / data-upstream-layer so the refusing layer survives to the DOM.

implementationPlan.description: TDD. Prove the edge is REAL rather than fixture-shaped, which is the failure mode this task exists to correct. The test must drive the PRODUCTION call site - render the live surface, feed it a frame through the feed's own transport seam, and assert the rendered phase lines - not call evaluateTiming directly and assert its return value, which is exactly what the existing command-latency.test.tsx already does and what left the production gap invisible. Assert the rendered receipt distinguishes all four phases by name, and assert at least one phase shows a real measured duration derived from observed values rather than from a literal the test supplied. Then assert the refusal arms end to end, each pinning the EXACT code AND the observer/layer that produced it: a daemon-seam UNKNOWN surfaces as TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN carrying the seam's own code, an unparseable reading as TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE, an absent observation as TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, a cross-clock pair as its explicit UNKNOWN, and no clock as TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE. Because two layers can refuse here, asserting only 'UNKNOWN' would stay green after the wrong layer starts answering first.
implementationPlan.note:
Live-path proof landed at apps/control-room/src/live/live-timing-path.test.tsx. 9 tests, all green.

SHAPE, which is the point: it renders LiveControlRoom (the real ?live=1 root), answers ONE poll through the feed's own transport seam via LiveSetup.transport.readEventPage, and reads the painted phase lines. It never calls evaluateTiming and asserts a return value - that is what command-latency.test.tsx already did while production had zero callers, and it is why the gap survived a green suite. Nothing here hands the surface a receipt, a duration or a reason code.

Deterministic without fake timers: the transport answers the first poll and leaves every later one pending, so the asserted surface is built from exactly one observed frame. The scripted clock returns 1_000 on its FIRST call and 1_030 on every later one. The first call is provably the feed's arrival reading, because LiveTimeline early-returns the waiting state while frame is null, so no render can read the clock before a frame lands.

MEASURED ARM: render = 30ms, observedBy CONTROL_ROOM, no unknown code. That 30 was subtracted by production between two readings it took at two moments; no literal 30 exists in the fixture.

REFUSAL ARMS, each pinning exact code AND producer:
- seam UNKNOWN -> unknownCode TIMING_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN, upstreamCode EVENT_STREAM_READING_NOT_PROVIDED, upstreamLayer SEAM, observedBy CONTROL_ROOM (the control room owns the stream interval even when the daemon is why it failed).
- unparseable daemon reading -> TIMING_SOURCE_UNPARSEABLE, observedBy DAEMON, and upstreamCode/upstreamLayer asserted ABSENT so this cannot be confused with a seam refusal.
- observation the frame never carried -> TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, observedBy DAEMON, upstreamCode asserted absent - this is the assertion that keeps "we never got it" distinct from "the seam refused".
- forward-skewed cross-clock pair -> TIMING_CLOCK_MISMATCH on both server (DAEMON) and stream (CONTROL_ROOM). Both readings parse and the seam reading is 200ms AFTER the ledger reading, so end < start is false and the skew guard cannot be what refused.
- no ClockProvider -> render TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE, no durationMs, upstreamCode absent.
- human -> TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT, no zero span.

Every arm also asserts durationMs is UNDEFINED, so no refusal can quietly carry a number.

implementationPlan.note:
Adversarial self-review. Skill loaded. All 7 plan checks answered by measurement, and the review FOUND A REAL DEFECT that I reproduced and fixed - see the deviation at the end.

(1) NO PATH SUBTRACTS ACROSS CLOCKS. There is exactly ONE subtraction in the entire path: timing.ts:193 `measured(observedBy, end - start)` inside fromInterval. The bridge never subtracts. fromInterval is reachable only through evaluateTiming, and `grep -rn "evaluateTiming(" apps packages --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx | grep -v "\.test\."` returns exactly TWO lines - its own definition and wire-timing.ts:212 - so buildLiveTimingReceipt is its only production caller. That call is fed only `sources.*.interval`, and pairing() returns an interval ONLY after `from.clock === to.clock`. The guard is structural, not merely tested: no cross-clock pair can reach the one subtraction. Drill 2 in step 7 confirms the negative-interval check is NOT a substitute.

(2) NO UNKNOWN BECOMES A NUMBER. No Math.abs, no Math.round, no reduce, no interpolation anywhere in timing.ts / wire-timing.ts / live-command-timing.tsx. TimingUnknown has no durationMs PROPERTY at all rather than a null one, and the step-6 sweep asserts `Object.hasOwn(resolved, "durationMs") === false` on all 22 refusal cases, so a refusal cannot carry a number even by accident.

(3) RENDER OBSERVATION IS FROM THE INJECTED CLOCK ON EVERY BRANCH. `const rendered = readClientClock(useClock())` sits at the top of the component, BEFORE the `rows.length === 0` early return - so it is unconditional (also correct React hook order; after the return it would have been a conditional hook call). Read during render, never stored in state, StrictMode-safe. No clock -> TIMING_CLOCK_UNAVAILABLE, asserted end to end.

(4) FOUR PHASES STAY SEPARATE. No sum, average or total in the rendered output. describeTimingReceipt returns one line per phase and deliberately no aggregate. The only comparison against a number is command-latency.tsx:138's pre-existing STILL_WORKING_THRESHOLD_MS on a SINGLE elapsed phase - not a collapse of the four.

(5) THE FEED SHAPES, IT DOES NOT INFER. identityOf refuses an empty commandId (`return null`) rather than minting an identity that names nothing; principal/run/session are shapeWireValue(...) so an absent one is null, not a stated empty; shapeWireObservation requires clock, observer AND reading and returns null otherwise. No invented truth class, no defaulted field.

(6) CLIENT PACKAGE AND GENERATED CLIENT UNTOUCHED BY MY DIFF. `git diff --stat ab45234..HEAD -- packages/control-room-client/src/generated/` is EMPTY. packages/control-room-client/src/client-transport.ts IS dirty, but it is a PEER's: the change is about the `Origin` fetch header and commit 79d9651 (task-702dcb63), nothing timing-related, and my plan never names it.

`testIdPrefix` was `cr.live.timing.<commandId>`. ONE COMMAND EMITS MANY EVENTS, so two rows of the same command painted two receipts - built from two DIFFERENT sets of readings - under one identical data-testid. planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
CROSS-CLOCK HANDLING - the sharpest decision in this plan, and the one most likely to be got wrong. The obvious approach is to lean on the landed skew guard: fromInterval already returns TIMING_NEGATIVE_INTERVAL when end < start, with a comment explaining that an absolute value would publish a confident number built from a contradiction. REJECTED AS SUFFICIENT: that guard catches only the half of cross-clock skew that happens to run negative. Skew in the other direction produces a positive, plausible, confidently WRONG duration and every test stays green. CHOSEN: compare the declared `clock` identities BEFORE subtracting and refuse a mismatched pair with an explicit UNKNOWN. The sibling put a `clock` field on WireObservation precisely so this is checkable; not using it would waste the field and leave the task's own rail ('do not compare cross-machine timestamps without an explicit shared observer or clock-offset uncertainty') satisfied only by luck. The negative-interval guard stays as a second line of defence.

UPSTREAM UNKNOWN - new code plus a carrier, rather than reuse. Mapping a WireUnknownValue onto the existing TIMING_SOURCE_ABSENT was considered and rejected: 'the daemon says it does not know' and 'we never received it' are different facts with different owners, and collapsing them destroys exactly the layer attribution the epic rail requires. Adding one code plus an optional upstream {code, layer} carrier keeps the seam's own code verbatim, matching how the event-stream seam already forwards store codes with no translation table.

WHERE THE REAL CALL SITE GOES. Candidates were live-board.tsx, live-app.tsx and recovery-actions.tsx. CHOSEN recovery-actions.tsx: it is the only production surface that already renders CommandLatency (with a Clock, at :241) and its feedback entries already carry commandId, so the receipt has something to attach to. This is the smallest change that produces a genuinely live edge rather than a demo one.

BRIDGE AS ITS OWN MODULE. Folding the wire-to-timing conversion into timing.ts was rejected: timing.ts is deliberately pure, reads no clock, and knows nothing of the wire; teaching it the seam vocabulary would couple the pure evaluator to the daemon's wire format. A separate bridge keeps evaluateTiming exactly as pure as it is now, and gives recovery-actions.tsx somewhere to move receipt assembly if it approaches the 250-line target.

NOT SPLIT. 8 files and 9 steps, inside both hard thresholds. The parent already SPIDR-split this work; splitting again would separate the bridge from its only consumer and leave a converter with nothing calling it.

planningNotes.risks:
THE PRODUCTION EDGE IS EASY TO FAKE. The existing command-latency.test.tsx already calls evaluateTiming directly and asserts the result - and that is precisely why the production gap survived a green suite for so long. A new test in that shape would prove nothing new. The step-5 test MUST drive the rendered surface through the feed, and the step-7 drill (bypass the production render timestamp) is what proves it did.

POSITIVE CROSS-CLOCK SKEW IS SILENT. See approachesConsidered. If the worker implements only the negative-interval guard, every test passes and the surface publishes wrong durations whenever the daemon clock runs behind the client's. A REFUSAL TEST CAN BE ANSWERED BY THE WRONG LAYER. There are now at least three places that can produce an UNKNOWN: the daemon seam, the bridge's parse, and the control room's missing clock. Asserting only 'known === false' stays green after the wrong one starts answering first. Every refusal assertion pins the exact code AND observer/layer.
